name: REST APIs and JSON
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Read and reason about REST API calls: verbs, URIs, status codes, authentication, data encodings and the JSON devices send back.

resources.title: Introducing JSON (json.org)
resources.note: The whole JSON grammar on one page, with syntax diagrams.

resources.title: HTTP response status codes (MDN)
resources.note: Every status code explained, with when servers send each one.

resources.title: HTTP request methods (MDN)
resources.note: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE, with which are safe and idempotent.

resources.title: Cisco DevNet learning labs
resources.note: Free guided labs that call real Cisco REST APIs, including always-on sandboxes.

resources.title: RFC 8040: RESTCONF protocol
resources.note: The standard behind /restconf/data URIs and the yang-data media types.

resources.title: Free CCNA 200-301 complete course (Jeremy's IT Lab)
resources.note: The REST API and JSON videos match this exam topic closely.

lesson.intro: Every controller, cloud dashboard and modern network device exposes a REST API that answers in JSON. The CCNA asks you to recognize how REST works and read JSON with confidence, and a software job asks the same on day one.
objectives: Map CRUD actions to HTTP verbs and predict which are safe and idempotent
Break a REST request into method, URI, headers and body, and read its status code
Compare basic, API key, bearer token and OAuth 2.0 authentication
Recognize JSON, XML and YAML, and identify objects, arrays, pairs and value types
Navigate a nested API response by hand and in Python

sections.title: What makes an API RESTful
sections.key: REST is an architectural style, not a protocol: client-server, stateless and cacheable, with resources named by URIs and nearly always carried over HTTPS.
sections.body:
You need the software version of 300 switches. Scraping `show version` over SSH breaks whenever the output format changes; the controller's API returns each device's `softwareVersion` as a named field.

[[visual]]

An **API** (application programming interface) is a contract for how one program asks another for data or actions. **REST** (Representational State Transfer, described by Roy Fielding in 2000) is a style for APIs. An API is **RESTful** when it follows these constraints:

[[visual 2]]

A REST API exposes **resources**: a device, an interface, the list of all devices. Each has a URI, and you act on it with a verb. Stateless does not mean the server stores nothing: it stores the resources, it just does not remember your last request.

Networking REST APIs nearly all run over **HTTPS**, because HTTP already works this way. Strictly, though, REST does not require HTTP.

items.title: CLI
points: `show version` over SSH, one switch at a time
The script must find the version inside them

items.title: REST API
points: The script reads a named field

visual.title: REST constraints
rows: The client (your script) asks; the server (a controller or device) answers
No session memory between requests: each one carries everything needed, credentials included
Responses say whether they may be cached, and for how long
Resources named by URIs, acted on with a few standard methods, sent as representations such as JSON
The client cannot tell whether proxies or load balancers sit in between
Optional: the server may send code for the client to run
visual.caption: Exam questions lean on the first three.

sections.tip: If a question asks which properties REST requires, pick client-server, stateless and cacheable. Do not pick "must use HTTP" or "must use JSON".
sections.pitfall: REST is a style, not a protocol, and JSON is not part of its definition. HTTP is the usual transport and JSON (or XML) the usual data format.

check.question: What does it mean that REST APIs are stateless?
choices: The server cannot store any data at all
Each request carries everything the server needs, such as the auth token, because the server keeps no session between requests
The API only supports GET requests
Responses can never be cached by the client
check.explanation: Statelessness is about requests, not storage. The server still holds resources, but it does not remember earlier requests, so each one must be complete on its own, credentials included.

sections.title: Anatomy of a REST call
sections.key: A REST request has a method, a URI naming the resource, headers carrying metadata and, for POST, PUT and PATCH, a body; the reply starts with a status code.
sections.body:
Here is a script asking Catalyst Center for one device. Every REST call has the same parts.

[[code]]

The **URI** (uniform resource identifier) names the resource:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The reply's JSON body is a **representation** of the resource: a copy of its current state as text, not the object itself. Underneath, it is plain HTTP inside TCP inside IP, the protocol your browser uses, read by a program instead of drawn on a screen.

Build requests against a mock API in the explorer below.

rows: Port 443 unless one follows the host: `https://10.10.20.48:8443/`
A name needs DNS; an IP address works too
`v1` is the API version. A path names a collection (`/vlans`) or one member (`/vlans/30`)
**Parameters** that filter or shape the result

visual.title: The rest of the request and reply
rows: What to do: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE
The format the client wants back, such as `application/json`
The format of the body being sent (and of most replies)
`Authorization`, or a vendor header such as `X-Auth-Token`
Data for POST, PUT and PATCH; GET and DELETE normally have none

sections.code:
import requests

base = "https://catc.example.com"
path = "/dna/intent/api/v1/network-device"
reply = requests.get(
    base + path,
    params={"managementIpAddress": "10.10.22.66"},
    headers={"Accept": "application/json",
             "X-Auth-Token": token},
)
print(reply.status_code)  # 200
device = reply.json()["response"][0]
print(device["hostname"])  # cat9k-access-1
sections.tip: Read API documentation like a menu: each resource lists its path, the methods it supports, the parameters it accepts and an example response.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting `Content-Type: application/json` on a POST or PUT is a classic bug. The server may reject the body with 415 Unsupported Media Type or misread it.

activity.title: Talk to a mock REST API
activity.prompt: Read the collection with GET, create an item with POST, then read, change and delete it. Compare the status codes you get for a read, a create and a delete. Then request a path that does not exist, or use a method the resource does not support, and read the error the server sends back.

check.question: In `https://catc.example.com/dna/intent/api/v1/network-device?hostname=SW1`, which part identifies the resource?
check.explanation: The path identifies the resource, here the network device list. The host names the server, and hostname=SW1 is a query parameter that filters the result.

sections.title: CRUD, HTTP verbs and idempotence
sections.key: POST creates, GET reads, PUT replaces, PATCH modifies and DELETE deletes. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so retrying them is harmless; retrying a POST can create duplicates.
sections.body:
Almost everything a program does with data is **CRUD**: Create, Read, Update or Delete.

[[visual]]

**PUT replaces** the whole resource with what you send; **PATCH modifies** only the fields you send. PUT an interface with just a new description and a strict server can drop what you left out, such as its IP address.

- **Safe** methods change nothing on the server: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS.
- **Idempotent** methods leave the same state whether sent once or ten times. PUT VLAN 30 five times and it exists once; DELETE it twice and it is still gone, though the second call may get 404.
- **POST is not idempotent**: each call usually creates a new member. PATCH is not guaranteed to be either.

Good automation retries when a reply is lost, so before resending a POST, check whether the first one worked.
sections.deeper:
Why PATCH is not idempotent in general: a patch can say "add this address to the list". Apply it twice and the list holds the address twice. A patch that just sets a field to a value happens to be idempotent, but the method does not promise it.

Some APIs bend the mapping: they create with PUT to a URI the client chooses, or update with POST. The CCNA expects the conventional mapping.
sections.tip: Exam shortcut: POST creates, GET reads, PUT and PATCH update, DELETE deletes.
sections.pitfall: Do not map POST to update or PUT to read on the exam. In code, never blindly retry a POST; you may create the same object twice.

check.question: A script times out waiting for the reply to `POST /api/v1/vlans` and sends the same request again. What risk does this create?
choices: The first VLAN is deleted and replaced by the second
The server returns 304 Not Modified and ignores the request
The VLAN may be created twice, because POST is not idempotent
check.explanation: The first POST may have succeeded even though the reply was lost. Because POST creates a new resource each time, the retry can create a duplicate. A PUT to a specific URI would be safe to repeat.

sections.title: Status codes: reading the reply
sections.key: The first digit says who to blame: 2xx success, 3xx look elsewhere, 4xx fix your request, 5xx the server failed. 401 means not authenticated; 403 means not allowed.
sections.body:
Before you touch the body, read the three-digit status code: it decides which branch of your script runs.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The 401 versus 403 distinction is a favorite. Despite its name, 401 is about **authentication** (who you are), and 403 is about **authorization** (what you may do).

Good automation follows the classes: treat 2xx as success, never retry a 4xx without changing something, and retry 429, 502 and 503 after a wait that grows each time (**exponential backoff**).

visual.title: 2xx success and 3xx redirection
rows: Here is what you asked for
A POST made a new resource; the `Location` header often gives its URI
It worked and there is no body, common after DELETE or PUT
The resource lives at another URI
Your cached copy is still current

visual.title: 4xx fix your request, 5xx the server failed
rows: No valid credentials: missing or expired token
Authenticated, but not allowed to do this
The resource exists, but not with that verb
Clashes with current state, such as creating something that exists
Internal error, bad gateway, service unavailable (503 is often temporary)

sections.tip: Memory hook: 2xx you did it, 4xx you got the request wrong, 5xx the server got it wrong.
sections.pitfall: A 2xx does not always mean the work is done. Catalyst Center answers many changes with 202 Accepted and a task ID to poll, and some APIs report errors inside a 200 body.

activity.title: Break it on purpose
activity.prompt: Trigger each error deliberately: post broken JSON or leave out a required field (400), ask for a task id that does not exist (404), use a method the path does not support such as DELETE on the whole collection (405), and send a body without the Content-Type: application/json header (415). Read the status line and the error body each time; real APIs explain themselves the same way.

check.question: A script with a valid token for a read-only account sends a DELETE request. Which status code fits best?
check.explanation: The server knows who the client is (valid token) but that account may not delete, so 403 Forbidden fits. 401 would mean the credentials were missing or invalid.

sections.title: Authentication: basic, API keys, tokens and OAuth
sections.key: Every stateless request must prove who you are: basic auth (only Base64, so HTTPS only), an API key, or a bearer token, often issued through OAuth 2.0.
sections.body:
The server forgets you after every request, so every request carries proof of identity.

[[visual]]

Basic auth turns `admin:secret` into `YWRtaW46c2VjcmV0`. That is encoding, not encryption: anyone who captures it decodes it in a second.

Cisco platforms use all three:

- **Catalyst Center**: basic auth once to get a token, then the token in an `X-Auth-Token` header on every call.
- **Meraki Dashboard API**: an API key sent as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.
- **RESTCONF on IOS XE**: basic auth over HTTPS on each request.

[[visual 2]]

Keep secrets out of scripts and source control: load them from environment variables or a vault, and use HTTPS everywhere.

rows: HTTPS only. Often used once, to get a token
A header such as `X-API-Key`, sometimes the query string
Store as a secret, rotate it, revoke it when it leaks or someone leaves. Query strings end up in logs
Expires; can be limited in scope
Whoever holds it can use it, like cash. When it expires, calls get 401
Issues the access token, used as a bearer token
An authorization server checks the client (and may ask a user to approve). The API never sees the password

visual.title: A token session with Catalyst Center

sections.tip: If a question says captured traffic reveals the password, think basic auth without TLS: Base64 is reversible.
sections.pitfall: A token or API key committed to a Git repository is a leaked credential, even if you delete the commit later. Revoke it and issue a new one.

activity.title: Prove who you are
activity.prompt: Call GET /api/me with no credentials and read the status code. Log in to get a token, add it as Authorization: Bearer <token>, and repeat the call. You have to send it on every request, because the server keeps no session for you. Finally use the same token on the admin endpoint and compare that 403 with the earlier 401.

check.question: Why must basic authentication only be used over HTTPS?
choices: The credentials are only Base64-encoded, so anyone who captures the request can decode them
Basic authentication only works on TCP port 443
HTTPS turns the password into a bearer token automatically
Plain HTTP cannot carry an Authorization header
check.explanation: Base64 is a reversible encoding with no key. Over plain HTTP the username and password cross the network readable by anyone who captures them; TLS encrypts the whole request, header included.

sections.title: Data encoding: JSON, XML and YAML
sections.key: JSON uses braces and brackets, XML uses opening and closing tags, YAML uses indentation. The data model (such as YANG) defines the data; the encoding is only how it travels.
sections.body:
A Python script and a Java controller hold data in memory differently, so they agree on a text format. The sender **serializes** its data to text and the receiver **parses** (deserializes) it back. The blueprint calls this **data encoding**.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Headers say which format is in play: `Content-Type` labels the body sent, and `Accept` asks for a format back. Ordinary APIs use `application/json` or `application/xml`; RESTCONF uses `application/yang-data+json` or `application/yang-data+xml`. Ask a RESTCONF server for XML and you get the same data, from the same YANG model, in a different encoding.

steps.label: **YAML**: `key: value` lines, indentation, `- ` for list items

rows: The default body of REST APIs
JavaScript Object Notation. Compact; maps onto dicts and lists in most languages
NETCONF; RESTCONF and many APIs offer it too
Extensible Markup Language. Verbose, one root element
YAML Ain't Markup Language. Most human-friendly; APIs rarely return it

sections.tip: Braces and brackets mean JSON, opening and closing tags mean XML, and indentation with no brackets means YAML.
sections.pitfall: Do not confuse the model with the encoding. YANG defines what the data is; JSON or XML is how it is written down. And XML has no number type: `<mtu>1500</mtu>` is text until a schema says otherwise.

check.question: A RESTCONF client changes its Accept header from application/yang-data+json to application/yang-data+xml. What changes in the reply?
choices: The server returns different data from a different YANG model
The same data, from the same YANG model, comes back encoded as XML instead of JSON
The request is now sent over NETCONF on port 830
Nothing, because Accept only affects requests that have a body
check.explanation: Accept chooses the encoding of the response. The YANG model defines the data either way, so only the format changes. NETCONF is a separate protocol, and Accept matters most on GET requests, which have no body.

sections.title: JSON building blocks and syntax rules
sections.key: JSON has objects (curly braces, double-quoted keys), arrays (square brackets), strings, numbers, true, false and null. Single quotes, trailing commas, comments and `True` are invalid.
sections.body:
JSON is small enough to learn completely.

[[visual]]

Objects and arrays nest to any depth: a device holds a list of interfaces, each with a list of addresses. Whitespace between elements is ignored, so pretty-printed (beautified) and minified JSON carry the same data.

[[code]]

Exam items show snippets and ask which one parses. These do not:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Every JSON value type
rows: Unordered `"key": value` pairs (key before the colon, value after), separated by commas. Keys are always double-quoted strings
Ordered list of values, separated by commas; types may mix
No quotes, no leading zeros, no hex

visual.title: Invalid JSON, and why
rows: Trailing comma after the last item
`True` is Python; JSON uses `true` (and `null`, never `NULL` or `None`)

sections.tip: Each colon outside a string marks exactly one key/value pair, so counting colons counts the pairs. Watch for colons inside strings, such as times or IPv6 addresses.
sections.pitfall: `"42"` and `42` are different types: a string and a number. `"true"` in quotes is a string, not a boolean. APIs are not always consistent, so check the quotes.

check.question: Which of these is valid JSON?
check.explanation: Keys and strings need double quotes, booleans are lowercase and unquoted, and there is no comma after the last pair. The other options break one of those rules.

sections.title: Reading a device API response
sections.key: Read nested JSON from the outside in, one key per object and one 0-based index per array, exactly the way code will index it.
sections.body:
This is a trimmed RESTCONF reply from an IOS XE router to `GET /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces` with `Accept: application/yang-data+json`. Its shape comes from a YANG model.

[[code]]

[[visual]]

So the path to the first address is `["ietf-interfaces:interfaces"]["interface"][0]["ietf-ip:ipv4"]["address"][0]["ip"]`: 10.10.20.48.

[[visual 2]]

RESTCONF is off by default. It runs inside the HTTPS server, so it needs `ip http secure-server` and `restconf`, plus AAA and a privilege 15 user for logins.

[[visual 3]]

root.label: `ietf-interfaces:interfaces`
root.sub: object; the YANG module prefixes the top key

children.label: `ietf-ip:ipv4`
children.sub: object: `mtu` (number) and `address`, an array of {ip, netmask} objects

visual.title: A RESTCONF URI, taken apart
rows: YANG module, a colon, then its top-level node
Not credentials and not a port
One entry, selected by its key
Narrows the reply to one interface
Unencoded, the slash reads as a path separator

items.title: Numbers in quotes
points: RESTCONF JSON (RFC 7951) sends 64-bit counters as strings

items.title: Empty, missing and null differ
points: No `description` key at all, as on GigabitEthernet2
Code that expects one crashes on another

sections.tip: To count objects, arrays or key/value pairs in an exam snippet, count `{`, `[` and `:` characters that are outside strings.
sections.pitfall: Arrays start at index 0. The first interface is `interface[0]`, so `interface[1]` is the second one.

activity.title: Take apart a RESTCONF reply
activity.prompt: Expand the tree and answer: how many interfaces are listed, which one is disabled, and what is the full path to Loopback0's IP address? Notice which values are strings, which are booleans and which is a number, and that address is an array even when it holds a single entry.

check.question: In this response, what is the value of `["ietf-interfaces:interfaces"]["interface"][1]["enabled"]`?
check.explanation: Index 1 is the second element of the interface array, GigabitEthernet2, and its enabled value is the boolean false.

sections.title: JSON drills: count it, path it, code it
sections.key: Count `{` for objects, `[` for arrays and colons outside strings for key/value pairs, and write paths one key or 0-based index per level.
sections.body:
Exam items about JSON are reading drills: how many objects, arrays or pairs, what sits at a path, which snippet is valid. A method beats staring. Take this document:

[[code]]

[[visual]]

Skip colons inside strings, such as times (`03:12:44`) and IPv6 addresses. Pairs belong to the object they sit in, so nested objects add their own. Skip a level, or index an object by number, and a path fails.

**In code** the same reading becomes indexing, because Python's `json.loads()` turns the text into dicts and lists:

[[visual 2]]

The playground parses a reply, loops over the devices and pulls out disabled interfaces and old software versions. Predict each line before you run it.

steps.label: Count `{` for objects
steps.note: the outer object and two interface objects

steps.label: Count `:` outside strings for pairs
steps.note: hostname, interfaces, then name and vlan twice

sections.tip: For any JSON exhibit: count { for objects, [ for arrays, and colons outside strings for key/value pairs.
sections.pitfall: The whole document is usually one object, so count the outermost `{` too. And an empty array `[]` still counts as an array, even with nothing in it.

activity.title: Walk an API response in Python
activity.prompt: Run it. json.loads() turns the reply into a dict holding a list, and the loop reads each device the way you would by hand. Before you change anything, predict what the path on the acc-sw7 line returns, then check.

props.code:
import json

reply = """{
  "response": [
    {"hostname": "core-sw1", "softwareVersion": "17.9.4", "reachable": true,
     "interfaces": [{"name": "Te1/0/1", "enabled": true},
                    {"name": "Te1/0/2", "enabled": false}]},
    {"hostname": "acc-sw7", "softwareVersion": "17.6.5", "reachable": true,
     "interfaces": [{"name": "Gi1/0/1", "enabled": true},
                    {"name": "Gi1/0/48", "enabled": false}]},
    {"hostname": "acc-sw8", "softwareVersion": "17.9.4", "reachable": false,
     "interfaces": []}
  ],
  "version": "1.0"
}"""

data = json.loads(reply)  # JSON text becomes Python dicts and lists
print(type(data).__name__, "holding", type(data["response"]).__name__)

devices = data["response"]
print("Devices:", len(devices))
print("First hostname:", devices[0]["hostname"])
print("acc-sw7 second interface:", data["response"][1]["interfaces"][1]["name"])

for dev in devices:
    down = [i["name"] for i in dev["interfaces"] if not i["enabled"]]
    flag = "" if dev["reachable"] else "  UNREACHABLE"
    print(f'{dev["hostname"]:9} {dev["softwareVersion"]:7} down: {down}{flag}')

old = [d["hostname"] for d in devices if d["softwareVersion"] != "17.9.4"]
print("Needs upgrade:", old)
props.task: Add a fourth device to the response list (remember the comma between objects) and predict the output first. Then print the path that reaches core-sw1's first interface name.

check.question: How many key/value pairs does `{"vlan": 10, "ports": ["Gi1/0/1", "Gi1/0/2"], "voice": {"vlan": 30}}` contain?
check.explanation: The outer object has three pairs (vlan, ports and voice), and the nested voice object has one more (vlan), so there are four colons outside strings and four pairs. The array holds values, not pairs.

keyTerms.definition: An architectural style for APIs: client-server, stateless, cacheable, with resources identified by URIs and a uniform interface.
The server keeps no session between requests, so each request carries everything needed, including credentials.
The identifier of a resource: scheme, host, path and an optional query string with parameters.
Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four basic data actions, mapped to POST, GET, PUT or PATCH, and DELETE.
Having the same effect whether a request is sent once or many times. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.
The three-digit result of an HTTP request: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
Username and password sent Base64-encoded in the Authorization header; safe only over HTTPS.
A credential sent as Authorization: Bearer <token> that grants access to whoever holds it, usually short-lived.
A long-lived secret issued to an application or user and sent with each request.
Converting in-memory data into a text format such as JSON or XML so another program can parse it.
Key/value pairs inside curly braces, with keys as double-quoted strings.
An ordered list of values inside square brackets.
The method of a request, such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE, saying what to do with the resource.
A framework in which an authorization server issues scoped, short-lived access tokens that clients present as bearer tokens.
The text format used to serialize data for transfer, such as JSON, XML or YAML.
A tag-based encoding with matching start and end tags inside one root element; used by NETCONF.
An indentation-based encoding with key: value lines and dash list items; used by Ansible.
A REST-style HTTPS API for YANG-modeled device data, carrying JSON or XML; enabled on IOS XE with restconf.

summary: REST is a style: client-server, stateless and cacheable, with resources named by URIs, nearly always over HTTPS.
POST creates, GET reads, PUT replaces, PATCH modifies, DELETE deletes; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent.
2xx success, 4xx fix your request (401 not authenticated, 403 not allowed), 5xx the server failed.
Basic auth is only Base64; API keys are long-lived; bearer tokens, often from OAuth 2.0, expire.
JSON uses braces and brackets, XML tags, YAML indentation; JSON keys are always double-quoted.
Count { for objects, [ for arrays and colons for pairs, and read paths from the outside in.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a network engineer who has only used the CLI how a script gets the device list from a controller's REST API: the request it sends, how it authenticates, what the status code tells it, and how to find a device's IP address in the JSON that comes back.

questions.question: Which HTTP verb maps to the CRUD Read action?
questions.explanation: GET retrieves a representation of a resource without changing it. POST creates, PUT and PATCH update.

questions.question: Match each CRUD action to the HTTP verb conventionally used for it.

pairs.left: Update by replacing the whole resource
Update by changing only some fields

questions.explanation: POST creates, GET reads, PUT replaces, PATCH modifies part of a resource and DELETE removes it. Some APIs bend the convention, so documentation has the final word.

questions.question: Which two are constraints of a REST API? Choose two.
choices: Must use HTTP as the transport
Must encode all data as XML
The server keeps a session for each client
questions.explanation: Client-server and stateless are core REST constraints (along with cacheable, uniform interface and layered system). HTTP is the usual transport but not a requirement, any data format may be used, and keeping per-client sessions contradicts statelessness.

questions.question: A client authenticated successfully one second ago, then sends a GET with no credentials or token. What does a stateless REST server do?
choices: Accepts it, because it remembers the earlier login
Rejects it, because it treats every request on its own and needs credentials on each one
Queues it until the client reconnects
Accepts it, because GET requests never need authentication
questions.explanation: A stateless server keeps no session between requests, so each request must carry its own credentials or token. That is why tokens are sent in a header on every call.

questions.question: Type the path (resource) part of this URI.
questions.explanation: The path runs from the first / after the host up to the ?. Everything after the ? is the query string with its parameters.

questions.question: What is the job of `?hostname=SW1&role=ACCESS` in this request?
choices: It is the query string, passing two parameters that filter the results
It is the path that identifies a resource named SW1
It is a header that authenticates the client
It is the JSON request body
questions.explanation: Text after the ? is the query string. Parameters are name=value pairs joined by &, and here they narrow the device list to access switches named SW1.

questions.question: A POST that creates a new VLAN succeeds. Which status code is the most specific success code for this result?
questions.explanation: 201 Created says a new resource now exists, and the Location header often gives its URI. 200 is a generic success, and 204 means success with no body.

questions.question: Match each status code to its meaning.

pairs.right: Success, and the body holds the result
Success, with no body to return
The request is malformed, such as invalid JSON
The requested resource does not exist
The server is temporarily unable to handle requests

questions.explanation: 2xx codes are successes, 4xx codes mean the client's request is at fault, and 5xx codes mean the server failed. 503 is often temporary, so a later retry can work.

questions.question: A script's API token expired an hour ago. Which status code will its next call most likely get?
questions.explanation: An expired token means the client is no longer authenticated, which is 401. The fix is to obtain a fresh token and retry. 403 would mean the server knows who you are but you lack permission.

questions.question: The server answers this request with 415 Unsupported Media Type. What should the engineer fix?
questions.code:
POST /api/v1/vlans HTTP/1.1
Host: sw-api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer 9f2c41d07a...
Content-Type: text/plain

{"id": 40, "name": "CAMERAS"}
choices: Change Content-Type to application/json so it describes the body
Wrap the body in square brackets
questions.explanation: 415 means the server will not accept the body's declared media type. The body is JSON but is labeled text/plain, so the header must say application/json. The token and the JSON itself are fine.

questions.question: A capture of an API call sent over plain HTTP shows this request. What can an attacker who captured it do?
questions.code:
GET /api/v1/devices HTTP/1.1
Host: 10.1.1.50
Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46c2VjcmV0
choices: Nothing, because Base64 encrypts the password
Decode the header to the username and password (admin:secret) and reuse them
Only replay this one request, because the value expires in seconds
Nothing, unless they also have the server's private key
questions.explanation: Basic auth is just username:password in Base64, which anyone can decode without a key. Over plain HTTP the credentials are exposed and reusable until the password changes. HTTPS would have encrypted the header.

questions.question: What does the word bearer in `Authorization: Bearer <token>` imply?
choices: The token is bound to one IP address and useless anywhere else
The token carries the user's password in encrypted form
The token is valid for a single request only
Whoever presents the token gets its access, so it must be protected like a password
questions.explanation: A bearer token works for anyone who holds it, like cash. That is why tokens travel only over HTTPS, expire, and must never be logged or committed to source control.

questions.question: Put the steps of a token-based session with Catalyst Center in order.
items: The script sends a POST to the token endpoint using basic authentication
Catalyst Center returns a token in a JSON body
The script sends a GET with the token in the X-Auth-Token header
Catalyst Center validates the token and returns 200 with the device list
The token expires and calls start returning 401
The script requests a new token and carries on
questions.explanation: Basic authentication is used once to get a token, which then rides on every request because the API is stateless. When it expires the server answers 401 and the client must log in again.

questions.question: Which statement best compares an API key with a token from a login flow?
choices: API keys are always encrypted, while tokens are always sent in plain text
API keys only work with GET, while tokens work with every verb
API keys are usually long-lived secrets tied to an app or user, while login tokens usually expire after a set time
API keys need no protection because they are not passwords
questions.explanation: API keys tend to live until someone revokes or rotates them, so a leaked key stays dangerous. Login tokens are short-lived by design. Both are secrets and both can be sent as bearer credentials.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is not idempotent?
questions.explanation: Sending the same POST twice usually creates two resources. GET, PUT and DELETE leave the server in the same state however many times you repeat them.

questions.question: Which three HTTP methods are idempotent? Choose three.
questions.explanation: GET changes nothing, PUT sets a resource to the same full state every time, and DELETE leaves it deleted. POST creates a new resource per call, and PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent.

questions.question: GigabitEthernet2 currently has a description and an IPv4 address. The engineer only wants to change the description and sends this request. What is the risk?
choices: PUT replaces the whole resource, so the IPv4 address, which is not in the body, can be removed
PUT merges fields, so there is no risk
PUT creates a second GigabitEthernet2 interface
questions.explanation: PUT means replace the target with exactly this representation, so anything left out can be deleted. PATCH would merge just the new description into the existing interface.

questions.question: A script needs to change only the description of an existing resource and leave every other field alone. Which method fits best?
questions.explanation: PATCH applies a partial modification, changing only the fields in the body. PUT would replace the whole resource, and POST normally creates a new one.

questions.question: In JSON, what do square brackets `[ ]` contain?
choices: An ordered list of values (an array)
questions.explanation: Square brackets hold an array, an ordered list of values. Curly braces hold an object of key/value pairs, and JSON has no comments.

questions.question: Which of these is a JSON boolean?
questions.explanation: JSON booleans are the lowercase, unquoted words true and false. "true" in double quotes is a string, True is Python syntax, and single quotes are never valid in JSON.

questions.question: A JSON parser rejects this document. What is wrong?
choices: There is a trailing comma after the last array element
questions.explanation: JSON does not allow a comma after the last element of an array or the last pair of an object. Booleans are correctly unquoted, and keys and array values may be any strings.

questions.question: Which description of this JSON is correct?
choices: One object with one key/value pair whose value is an array
One object with three key/value pairs
An array that contains one object
One object whose value is a second object
questions.explanation: The outer braces make one object, and the single colon means one key/value pair. Its value, in square brackets, is an array of three numbers.

questions.question: Which two of these are values, not keys? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Keys sit before a colon and values after it. "ACCESS" and "10.10.22.66" follow colons, while response, type and managementIpAddress are keys.

questions.question: What is the JSON data type of the value of interfaceCount?
questions.explanation: The value is in double quotes, so it is a string even though it looks like a number. Code that does arithmetic on it must convert it first.

questions.question: Which path returns "10.10.21.48"?
questions.explanation: 10.10.21.48 is the second address (index 1) of the first interface (index 0). Arrays are indexed by position before you can use a key, and you cannot skip levels of nesting.

questions.question: Match each JSON value to its type.
questions.explanation: Double quotes make a string, bare digits a number, true or false a boolean, null the absence of a value, square brackets an array and curly braces an object.

questions.question: What Python types does `data` contain after this line runs?
questions.code:
import json
data = json.loads(reply_text)   # reply_text holds a JSON object containing an array
choices: One long str, because JSON is text
questions.explanation: Python's json module maps JSON objects to dicts and arrays to lists (and true, false and null to True, False and None), so you navigate the result with normal indexing.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Accept and Content-Type headers in a REST request?
choices: Accept carries credentials; Content-Type carries the URI
Accept says which format the client wants back; Content-Type says which format the body is in
They are two names for the same header
Accept is set by the server; Content-Type only appears in responses
questions.explanation: Accept negotiates the response format, for example application/json. Content-Type labels the body actually being sent, in requests that have a body and in most responses.

questions.question: Which two data formats do REST APIs used for network automation most commonly return? Choose two.
questions.explanation: JSON is the default, and many APIs (RESTCONF among them) also offer XML. YAML is common for configuration files such as Ansible playbooks but rarely as an API response, and JavaScript is a programming language, not a data format.

questions.question: `GET /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=GigabitEthernet1` works, but the same request for `interface=GigabitEthernet1/0/1` on a switch returns an error. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Put the interface name in the request body instead
Ask for XML instead of JSON in the Accept header
URL-encode the slashes in the interface name as %2F
questions.explanation: A / in the name is read as a path separator, so the server looks for the wrong resource. Encoding it as GigabitEthernet1%2F0%2F1 keeps the name as one value.

questions.question: What does it mean for a REST API to be stateless, and what does that mean for authentication?
questions.answer: The server keeps no session memory between requests, so each request must carry everything needed to process it. Credentials or a token therefore have to be sent with every request.
questions.explanation: This is why APIs use headers like Authorization or X-Auth-Token on each call instead of a login session.

questions.question: Which data encoding is this?
questions.explanation: Matching start and end tags in angle brackets mark XML. JSON uses braces and quoted keys, and YAML uses indented key: value lines with no brackets.

questions.question: Match each format or language to where you usually meet it.

pairs.right: Default body format of REST APIs
Defines the data model, whatever the encoding

questions.explanation: JSON dominates REST, NETCONF speaks XML, and Ansible is written in YAML. YANG is not an encoding at all; it models the data that JSON or XML then carry.

questions.question: A script wants a RESTCONF server to reply in XML. Which header should it send?
questions.explanation: Accept tells the server which format the client wants back, and RESTCONF uses the yang-data media types. Content-Type describes a body the client is sending, and Authorization carries credentials.

questions.question: Which two statements about data serialization are true? Choose two.
choices: The sender serializes its in-memory data into text such as JSON or XML
The receiver parses that text back into its own data structures
JSON can only be parsed by programs written in JavaScript
Serializing data to JSON encrypts it
XML and JSON cannot represent the same data
questions.explanation: Serialization turns data into a shared text format and parsing turns it back, which lets programs in different languages exchange data. Every major language parses JSON, encoding is not encryption, and the same data can be written in either XML or JSON.

questions.question: The HTTPS server is already enabled on an IOS XE router. Type the global configuration command that enables the RESTCONF service.
questions.explanation: restconf turns on the RESTCONF API, served by the HTTPS server that ip http secure-server enables. Logins also need AAA and a privilege 15 user.

questions.question: An engineer applied this configuration, but every RESTCONF request to R1 fails with connection refused on TCP port 443. What is missing?
questions.code:
! Configuration applied to R1
aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default local
aaa authorization exec default local
username api privilege 15 secret Str0ngPa55
no ip http secure-server
restconf
choices: Enable ip http secure-server, because RESTCONF is served by the HTTPS server
Lower the api user to privilege 1
Add ip http server, because RESTCONF uses plain HTTP on port 80
questions.explanation: RESTCONF runs inside the device HTTPS server, and no ip http secure-server turns that server off, so nothing listens on 443. netconf-yang enables a different protocol, privilege 15 is what RESTCONF logins need, and RESTCONF should never run over plain HTTP.

questions.question: In `https://10.10.20.48/restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=Loopback0`, what does `ietf-interfaces:interfaces` identify?
choices: The YANG module (ietf-interfaces) and its top-level container (interfaces)
A username and password separated by a colon
The TCP port the API listens on
A query parameter that filters interfaces
questions.explanation: RESTCONF data URIs name the YANG module, a colon, then the node inside it. interface=Loopback0 then selects one list entry by its key. Credentials go in headers, the port would follow the host, and query parameters come after a ?.

questions.question: How many JSON objects are in this document?
questions.explanation: Count the { characters: the outermost object, the device object and the two interface objects make four. The two arrays (interfaces and ntp) are not objects.

questions.question: How many key/value pairs are in this document?
questions.explanation: The outer object has four pairs (hostname, uptime, mgmt and uplinks) and mgmt has two (ip and vlan). There are eight colons, but the two inside the uptime string are text, not separators.

questions.question: After `data = json.loads(reply)` runs on this reply, which expression returns "acc-sw7"?
questions.explanation: data is a dict; data["response"] is the list of devices; index 1 is the second device, acc-sw7; and ["hostname"] reads its name. A list must be indexed by position before a key can be used, and data itself is not a list.

questions.question: Which description of this JSON is correct?
questions.explanation: There are three { (the outer object and two VLAN objects), one [ (vlans), and four colons outside strings: vlans, id, id and trunk. The inner objects count too.

questions.question: A JSON parser rejects this document. What is wrong?
choices: The IP address must be a number, not a string
There is no comma after "R2", between the first and second pairs
Booleans must be written in quotes
questions.explanation: Pairs in an object are separated by commas, and the first pair is missing its comma. Addresses are normally strings, true is correctly unquoted, and any string can be a key.

questions.question: In OAuth 2.0, what does the client send to the API on each request?
choices: The user's username and password in Base64
A client certificate and nothing else
An access token issued by an authorization server, usually as a bearer token
Nothing, because the API keeps a session after the first login
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 separates login from API access: an authorization server issues a short-lived, scoped access token, and the client presents it as Authorization: Bearer <token>. The API never sees the password, and REST APIs keep no session.

questions.question: A script sends DELETE /api/v1/devices and gets 405 Method Not Allowed. What does that tell it?
choices: The resource exists, but it does not support the DELETE method
questions.explanation: 405 means the path is valid but not for that verb; the API refuses to delete the whole device collection. An expired token gives 401, a malformed body 400, and a server failure 5xx.
